what_building.ask: What are you building, in a sentence or two?
what_building.why: Everything else builds on this. It becomes the description in PROJECT.md.
examples: A booking app for a small physiotherapy clinic
An internal API that prices insurance quotes
A portfolio site for a photographer

project_status.ask: Where does the project stand today: an idea, being designed, being built, live, or in maintenance?
project_status.why: It tells everyone how settled the documents should be.

project_owner.ask: Who makes the final calls on this project, if anyone besides you?

project_constraints.ask: Is anything limiting the work: a deadline, a budget, team size, or a platform or regulatory commitment?
project_constraints.why: Constraints shape what is realistic before any design starts. 'None that matter yet' is a fine answer.
examples: Must launch before the September intake
One developer, evenings only
Has to run on the client's existing Azure account

profile_fit.ask: Which of these describes what the system does: publishes content people read, lets people do work with their own data, provides services other software depends on, or produces results with AI models at run time?
profile_fit.why: Groundwork's profiles add the documents each kind of system needs. They are chosen by what the system does, never by the technology.
profile_fit.explain: A profile is a bundle of documents and checks for one kind of system: web, application, backend-api and ai-systems. Several can apply at once.

problem.ask: What problem are people having today that this should solve?
problem.why: Starting from the problem keeps the product from turning into a list of features nobody needs.
examples: Members track savings contributions in a shared spreadsheet and errors go unnoticed
Visitors can't find opening hours on the current site

existing_alternatives.ask: How do people deal with it now, and what's wrong with that?
existing_alternatives.why: The current workaround shows what the product must beat.

primary_users.ask: Who will use it most, and what are they trying to get done?

user_types.ask: Are there other kinds of people involved, such as administrators, staff, partners or people who pay, with different needs or permissions?
user_types.why: Different kinds of users usually mean different screens, rules and permissions.

desired_outcomes.ask: If this works, what is different for the people using it, and for you or the business?
examples: A member checks their balance without asking the treasurer
Support resolves requests faster
A visitor finds what they need and gets in touch

capabilities.ask: What are the main things people must be able to do with it?
capabilities.why: Each becomes a capability with a CAP- ID that requirements and tests trace back to.

scope_in.ask: What must the first version include?

scope_out.ask: What are you deliberately leaving out, at least for now?
scope_out.why: Writing exclusions down stops them creeping back in.

key_journeys.ask: Walk me through the most important thing someone does, from start to finish.
key_journeys.why: End-to-end journeys become the critical tests later.

success_measures.ask: How would you know it's working? Is there anything you could count or observe?
examples: Weekly active members
Time to answer a support request
Enquiries per month from the site

product_risks.ask: What could make this fail, or what are you assuming is true that you haven't checked?
examples: Members are willing to switch from the spreadsheet
The payment provider approves us in time

functional_requirements.ask: From the capabilities, here are the testable requirements I would write. Do they match what you intend?
functional_requirements.why: Requirements are what the system must do, written so a test can prove it. The agent drafts them from the PRD; you confirm them.

quality_expectations.ask: Are there expectations about how well it must work: speed, availability, accessibility, privacy, or how many people use it at once?
quality_expectations.why: These become non-functional requirements: qualities rather than features.
quality_expectations.explain: A non-functional requirement describes how well the system works rather than what it does, for example 'pages load in under two seconds'.
examples: Usable on a cheap phone over a slow connection
Meets WCAG 2.2 AA
Must stay up during exam week

system_constraints.ask: Are there technical limits the system must respect: existing systems, required platforms, hosting rules, or technology you've already committed to?
system_constraints.why: Only real constraints belong here. Preferences can wait until the design is clearer.

business_rules.ask: Are there rules the system must always follow, whatever the screen or feature?
business_rules.explain: A business rule is a rule from the real world the software must enforce, such as 'a loan can't exceed twice a member's savings'.

acceptance_criteria.ask: For the system as a whole, what must be true before you'd call a release acceptable?

architecture_known.ask: Do you already know roughly how it will be built, for example one app, an app plus a backend, or several services? Or should we work that out from the requirements?
architecture_known.why: Not knowing yet is fine. The architecture should follow from what the system must do.

external_systems.ask: What outside systems or services does it talk to or depend on?
examples: A payment provider
The company's single sign-on
An email service
A government API

cross_cutting.ask: Are there concerns that touch the whole system, such as privacy, compliance, accessibility or performance, that the design must account for everywhere?

key_decisions.ask: Have any significant technical decisions already been made, and why?
key_decisions.why: Decisions that are expensive to reverse get an ADR, a short record of the decision and its reasons.

agent_code_standards.ask: Are there coding conventions the agent should follow: naming, layout, how errors and types are handled?

tooling.ask: Which tools format, lint, type-check and test the code, and which must pass in CI?

build_prerequisites.ask: What does someone need installed, and how do they set up, run and test the project locally?

security_scope.ask: What in this system is worth protecting: personal data, money, accounts, secrets, or availability?
security_scope.why: Security effort should match what is actually at risk.

access_model.ask: How do people sign in, and who is allowed to see or change what?
access_model.explain: Authentication is proving who someone is. Authorisation is deciding what they may do.

sensitive_data.ask: What sensitive data does it handle, where is it stored, and who must never see it?
sensitive_data.why: Only describe the kinds of data. Never paste real secrets, passwords or keys here.

interface_threats.ask: Where does untrusted input enter the system, and what would an attacker most want to do?
interface_threats.explain: A trust boundary is where data crosses from something you don't control (a browser, a partner, the internet) into something you do.

dependency_policy.ask: How are third-party libraries and services chosen, updated and checked for known problems?

security_logging.ask: What security events must be logged, and who responds when something goes wrong?

security_verification.ask: How will security be checked: reviews, automated scans, tests of permission rules?

quality_objectives.ask: What would hurt most if it broke? Which parts need the most confidence?
quality_objectives.why: Testing effort follows risk. Tools come later.

test_layers.ask: Roughly how should testing be split: fast unit tests, tests that use real dependencies, end-to-end tests of whole journeys?
test_layers.explain: Unit tests check one small piece in isolation. Integration tests check pieces working together. End-to-end tests drive the whole system like a user would.

critical_scenarios.ask: Which journeys and failure cases must always be tested before a release?

test_data.ask: What test data and environments are needed, and is any of it sensitive?

release_gates.ask: What must pass before a change can ship?

repository_layout.ask: Will the parts of the system be built, deployed and owned together, or separately?
repository_layout.why: Start with the simplest layout that handles real constraints: one app, a monorepo, or several repositories.
repository_layout.applies_when: The repository has more than one deployable part, or the layout is being chosen.

domain_concepts.ask: What are the main things the system keeps track of, and how do they relate?
domain_concepts.explain: These are the nouns of the system, such as Member, Contribution and Loan, and the links between them.
examples: A member has many contributions
A booking belongs to one clinician and one patient

state_lifecycle.ask: Do any of those things move through stages, and what moves them along?
examples: A loan goes from requested to approved to repaid
An order goes from placed to paid to shipped

data_ownership.ask: Who owns each kind of data, how long is it kept, and can it be deleted?

invariants.ask: Which rules must never be broken, even if two people act at the same moment?
invariants.explain: An invariant is a rule that must always hold, such as 'a balance never goes below zero'.

triggers.ask: What starts each important operation: a person, a schedule, another system, a payment arriving?

validation_rules.ask: What input is rejected, and what must be true before and after each important operation?

components.ask: What are the main parts of the system and what is each responsible for?

communication.ask: How do the parts talk to each other and to outside systems: direct requests, messages, shared data?

technology_choices.ask: Which technologies have been chosen, and what drove each choice?
technology_choices.why: Record choices once they are made, with their reasons. Groundwork never picks technology for you.

runtime_model.ask: What runs where, and does anything happen in the background or at the same time as something else?

failure_handling.ask: What happens when something fails part-way: a payment times out, a server restarts, a message is delivered twice?
failure_handling.explain: Idempotency means doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once, which makes retries safe.

recovery.ask: How does the system recover, and how much data loss or downtime is acceptable?

operating_model.ask: Who deploys and runs the system, and on what kind of hosting?

observability.ask: How will you know it is healthy, and how will you find out what went wrong?
observability.explain: Observability is the logs, metrics and traces that let you see what a running system is doing.

scaling.ask: How much use do you expect, and how should it cope with growth or spikes?

ui_surfaces.ask: What screens or views are there, and which kinds of users see each?

interaction_mapping.ask: For the important screens, which user actions change data or start work in the system?

experience_principles.ask: How should using the product feel? Pick a few words or principles.
examples: Calm and trustworthy
Fast for experts, forgiving for beginners
Playful but never confusing

brand_identity.ask: Is there an existing brand (logo, colours, typefaces), or are we creating a visual direction from scratch?
brand_identity.applies_when: The product has a visual identity to define or follow.

design_tokens.ask: Do you need shared design tokens, the named colours, sizes and spacing that keep screens consistent, or are a few documented values enough for now?
design_tokens.explain: A design token is a named value such as color.text.primary that designers and code both use.

component_conventions.ask: Are you using an existing component library, or building your own components?

ux_states.ask: How should screens behave while loading, when empty, and when something fails?

accessibility.ask: Which accessibility standard should the interface meet, and which devices and screen sizes must it support?
examples: WCAG 2.2 AA on phone and desktop
Keyboard-only use for the admin area

information_architecture.ask: How is the product organised: main areas, navigation, and how people find things?

design_governance.ask: Who owns design decisions, and where does the source of truth for designs live?
design_governance.applies_when: More than one person designs or builds the interface.

contract_consumers.ask: Which interfaces do other teams, partners or separately released clients depend on, and how will changes stay compatible?
contract_consumers.explain: A contract is the written promise of how an interface behaves, so consumers can rely on it while it changes.

PROJECT.md.purpose: The cover page: project identity, status, constraints and active profiles. Product substance lives in the PRD.
PROJECT.md.skip: Keep the file. The name and description come from create-groundwork; record the rest when known.

sections.heading: The basics
sections.done_when: Name, description and status are filled in, and the owner if there is one.

sections.heading: Project constraints
sections.done_when: Known limits are recorded, or the section says there are none yet.

sections.heading: Profiles
sections.done_when: The Profiles line names the profiles the developer agreed to, and Why explains the choice by what the system does.

docs/product/PRD.md.purpose: The source of truth for product intent: the problem, users, outcomes, capabilities, scope and success measures. No implementation detail.
docs/product/PRD.md.skip: A required document: if skipped, it stays in place and is reported as incomplete. Work proceeds from what the developer says, and gaps are flagged when they matter.

sections.heading: Problem
sections.done_when: The problem is stated without naming a solution, together with how people cope today.

sections.heading: Users and stakeholders
sections.done_when: The main users and any other affected groups are named, with what each needs.

sections.heading: What success looks like
sections.done_when: Outcomes describe results for users and the business, not features.

sections.heading: Product capabilities
sections.done_when: Each capability has a CAP-NNN ID, a description, why users care and a priority, and the developer has confirmed the list.

sections.heading: Scope
sections.done_when: In scope and out of scope are both listed and confirmed.

sections.heading: Key user journeys
sections.done_when: The important end-to-end journeys are described in steps.

sections.heading: How we'll measure success
sections.done_when: Each measure has a target and a way to measure it, or is marked unknown.

sections.heading: Risks, assumptions and dependencies
sections.done_when: Known risks and untested assumptions are listed.

sections.heading: Open questions
sections.done_when: Unresolved product questions are listed, each with who can answer it.

docs/product/SPEC.md.purpose: Testable, system-wide requirements with stable IDs, derived from the approved PRD.
docs/product/SPEC.md.skip: Required: if skipped, it is reported as incomplete. Feature specs can still be written; they then carry the requirements themselves.

sections.heading: 1. Purpose
sections.done_when: States what the system is for, referring to the PRD rather than repeating it.

sections.heading: 2. System Scope
sections.done_when: System boundaries follow the PRD scope.

sections.heading: 3. System Context
sections.done_when: Users and outside systems the system interacts with are named.

sections.heading: 4. System-Wide Functional Requirements
sections.done_when: Each requirement has a stable ID, names the capability it serves, is testable, and has been confirmed.

sections.heading: 5. Non-Functional Requirements
sections.done_when: Quality expectations are measurable, or explicitly unknown with a note.

sections.heading: 6. System Constraints
sections.done_when: Real constraints are listed; preferences are not.

sections.heading: 7. Global Business Rules
sections.done_when: Rules that apply everywhere are listed with IDs and confirmed.

sections.heading: 8. Global Acceptance Criteria
sections.done_when: System-wide release criteria are listed and confirmed.

sections.heading: 9. Feature Specification Index
sections.done_when: Every feature spec in docs/product/specs/ is listed.

sections.heading: 10. Open Questions
sections.done_when: Unresolved requirement questions are listed.

docs/architecture/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md.purpose: The architecture starting point and index: the system's shape, context, cross-cutting concerns and key decisions. Detail lives in system-design/.
docs/architecture/SYSTEM_DESIGN.md.skip: Required: if skipped, it is reported as incomplete. Architecture is recorded once the requirements justify it.

sections.heading: Summary
sections.done_when: The system's shape is summarised, or the summary says what is still undecided and what it depends on.

sections.heading: Context and high-level view
sections.done_when: Users, outside systems and the system boundary are described.

sections.heading: Cross-cutting concerns
sections.done_when: Concerns that touch the whole system are named, with where each is handled.

sections.heading: Key decisions
sections.done_when: Each significant decision links to an ADR.

sections.heading: Open questions and risks
sections.done_when: Undecided architecture questions are listed.

AGENTS.md.purpose: How agents work in this repository: rules, code standards, tooling, workflow and definition of done.
AGENTS.md.skip: Keep the defaults until code exists; fill in standards and tooling when the first code is written.

sections.heading: Code standards
sections.done_when: The placeholder guidance is replaced with the project's conventions.

sections.heading: Tooling
sections.done_when: Every row names a tool and whether it must pass in CI, or says why it doesn't apply.

BUILD.md.purpose: How to set up, run and test the project locally.
BUILD.md.skip: Fill in once there is something to run.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
sections.done_when: A new developer could install what's needed from this list.

sections.heading: Setup
sections.done_when: Setup steps are listed and have been run once.

sections.heading: Run locally
sections.done_when: The command to run the project locally is listed.

sections.heading: Test
sections.done_when: The commands to run the tests are listed.

docs/engineering/SECURITY.md.purpose: Security requirements proportionate to what is at risk: access, data protection, input, dependencies, logging and verification.
docs/engineering/SECURITY.md.skip: If a profile requires it, skipping leaves it incomplete. In a core-only project with nothing worth attacking, mark it not applicable and delete it.

sections.heading: Objectives and scope
sections.done_when: What is protected, and from whom, is stated and confirmed.

sections.heading: Identity and access
sections.done_when: Sign-in and permission rules are described and confirmed, or the section says there are no accounts.

sections.heading: Data protection
sections.done_when: Kinds of sensitive data, where they live and how they are protected are described. No real secrets.

sections.heading: Input and interface security
sections.done_when: Trust boundaries and the main threats at each are listed.

sections.heading: Dependencies and supply chain
sections.done_when: How dependencies are chosen, updated and scanned is stated.

sections.heading: Logging and incident response
sections.done_when: Security events to log and who responds are named.

sections.heading: Verification
sections.done_when: How security is checked is listed.

docs/engineering/TEST_STRATEGY.md.purpose: What needs testing, at which layers, with which data, and what must pass before release. Tools follow the strategy.
docs/engineering/TEST_STRATEGY.md.skip: If a profile requires it, skipping leaves it incomplete; fill it in when the first tests are written.

sections.heading: Quality objectives
sections.done_when: The areas needing the most confidence are named.

sections.heading: Test layers
sections.done_when: What each layer covers is stated.

sections.heading: Critical scenarios
sections.done_when: Journeys and failure cases that must always be tested are listed, with requirement IDs.

sections.heading: Test data and environments
sections.done_when: Test data sources are described, and sensitive data is kept out of tests.

sections.heading: Release gates
sections.done_when: Checks that block a release are listed.

docs/architecture/REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.m.purpose: How the repository is laid out and why: module boundaries, ownership and dependency direction.
docs/architecture/REPOSITORY_STRUCTURE.m.skip: Mark not applicable and delete it once the layout is settled and obvious.

sections.heading: Single application
sections.applies_when: Everything is built and deployed together.
sections.done_when: The chosen layout is kept and the alternatives are removed.

sections.heading: Modular monorepo
sections.applies_when: Several apps or packages share one repository.
sections.done_when: Apps and packages are named with their owners and dependency direction.

sections.heading: Multiple repositories
sections.applies_when: Parts are owned or released separately.
sections.done_when: Each repository is named with its owner and what it contains.

docs/architecture/system-design/01-syste.purpose: What the system is and where its boundaries lie: actors, capabilities, scope and external systems.
docs/architecture/system-design/01-syste.skip: Required by some profiles; otherwise keep the summary in SYSTEM_DESIGN.md instead.

sections.heading: Purpose
sections.done_when: Summarises the purpose, referring to the PRD.

sections.heading: Actors and stakeholders
sections.done_when: Every person or system that acts on the system is named.

sections.heading: Core capabilities
sections.done_when: Links to the CAP- IDs in the PRD rather than restating them.

sections.heading: Scope and boundaries
sections.done_when: What is inside and outside the system is clear.

sections.heading: External systems and dependencies
sections.done_when: Each outside system is listed with what it is used for.

docs/architecture/system-design/02-domai.purpose: The things the system keeps track of, how they relate, who owns them and how their state changes.
docs/architecture/system-design/02-domai.skip: Required by some profiles; otherwise mark not applicable when the system keeps no data of its own.

sections.heading: Domain concepts
sections.done_when: The main concepts are defined in plain language, using names that match the code.

sections.heading: State model
sections.done_when: States and what moves things between them are listed.

sections.heading: Data structures and persistence
sections.done_when: Who owns each kind of data and how long it is kept is stated.

docs/architecture/system-design/03-behav.purpose: What the system must do and the rules it must preserve: operations, triggers, business rules and invariants.

sections.heading: Use cases and operations

sections.done_when: What starts each important operation is stated.

sections.heading: Business rules
sections.done_when: Rules are listed with IDs, referring to SPEC.md where they are global.

sections.heading: Invariants

sections.heading: Validation and constraints

sections.heading: Communication
sections.done_when: How components and outside systems talk is described.

sections.heading: Integrations

sections.heading: Technology choices
